There are a few principles potentially at work here.

Principle #1 - Perception is reality. If the adversary perceives that the target is stronger, then the reality is that they may believe it. Fences with razor wire around facilities is a good example. If those fences are well-maintain (i.e., no trash collecting on them; fences in good order), then the adversary may believe the target is stronger. Of course, if the adversary looks further and no additional security measures are evident, that perception may be disregarded.

Principle #2 - Display stronger security, enough to make the adversary pick a weaker target. How much security is enough? Security measures are costly and organizations are constantly evaluating how much is enough. Well... it is enough to make the adversary attack a weaker target. But, how do you know it is enough? Sometimes you do not know until the adversary breaches your security measures. It is a calculated risk.
